text.p: Brazil's soccer corruption inquiry starts on Wednesday and the game's authorities said the scandal could end up in a criminal court.
A group of Congressmen, who have began their own separate investigation, said they may recommend that telephone bills and bank accounts of those involved be examined.
At the same time, the Brazilian Football Confederation (CBF) has called in four former leading referees to sort out its discredited refereeing department and make it more accountable.

The scandal erupted last week with allegations that Ivens Mendes, head of the CBF's refereeing department, had used his post to exchange favours with club directors to fuel his campaign to be elected to the Brazilian Congress.
Mendes resigned amid media allegations he had offered to ask a referee to give Atletico Paranaense a helping hand in a Copa Brasil match they were to play in exchange for 25,000 Real ($23,600).

Carlos Antonio Navega, who is leading the CBF's inquiry, said he would begin work on Wednesday by summoning Mendes. "I don't have the power to oblige him to appear, but if he doesn't turn up it will count against him," he said.
"If there are signs that common crimes have been committed, then the matter could go to a criminal court." The inquiry is likely to take two to three weeks.
The Congressmen, who used parliamentary powers to open their own investigation, began their inquiry on Monday by interviewing Corinthians president Alberto Dualib, who said he had nothing to hide.

"He (Mendes) asked me to help his candidacy. Any club president, knowing he (Mendes) has been there for nine years, can't just turn him down flat," Dualib said. "He took a few (soccer) shirts, that was it."

Lindberg Farias, leader of the congressional committee, said their findings could be sent to the Public Prosecutor's Office, known as Public Ministery in Brazil, along with recommendations to investigate phone calls and bank accounts of the accused.

CBF president Ricardo Teixeira, who has publicly admitted he made a mistake by giving Mendes too much power, has begun rebuilding the refereeing department with some of the most- respected names in Brazilian refereeing.
"There is going to be a total revolution," promised former referee Armando Marques, one of those called in.
From Brazil's President Fernando Henrique Cardoso down, the country has been shocked by the scandal.
Although only one match has been specifically mentioned, Brazilians have been wondering how many other games could have been affected.

"I'm certain this was just the tip of the iceberg," said Zico, one of the great Brazilian players of the past and a former government sports minister. "I'm sure a lot of people were involved and they have to be eliminated from football."
